doc.title: Jones Hank — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Wells' restaurant and Teddie keeping Hank's books
summary: Teddie recalls Wells's ambitions and, with an accountant relative, kept Hank's books for years.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Now, the Wells’ is an institution in the Harlem community. Yes?
Yes, it is well known. He used to work for some official from…
They always used to call him the king or the prince (laughs). It was some title.
Yes, it was some unofficial title, actually right? But his employer, was he a state employee? He wasn’t a city employee, so he must have been state.
Yes, he was something like 60. He worked over there in England or something. That’s why…
Wells didn’t work for him but he was more like a confidant. They had a business relationship. I guess he helped him out on certain legal matters or what not.
He wanted to depend on Wells brain. Wells… was running a restaurant when he was in his teens. He was that ambitious.
Over the course of your husband’s career, giving him background in accounting and being in the business and away, have you been able to lend some of that expertise to his career?

Well, if I could interject, I think she had a lot to do with it. Not only was she Wells’ bookkeeper, she started keeping my books as well. She kept everything in order along with an accountant who is a relative. Between Mr. Singleton and her, they kept my books in perfect order for years.
When you get older, you start to think just how valuable it was.
